title: The Teacher Tests Pleasure and Great Works

verses.text: I said to myself, "Come now, I will test you with pleasure; enjoy what is good!" But it proved to be futile.
I said of laughter, "It is folly," and of pleasure, "What does it accomplish?"
I sought to cheer my body with wine and to embrace folly—my mind still guiding me with wisdom—until I could see what was worthwhile for men to do under heaven during the few days of their lives.
I expanded my pursuits. I built houses and planted vineyards for myself.
I made gardens and parks for myself, where I planted all kinds of fruit trees.
I built reservoirs to water my groves of flourishing trees.
I acquired menservants and maidservants, and servants were born in my house. I also owned more herds and flocks than anyone in Jerusalem before me,
and I accumulated for myself silver and gold and the treasure of kings and provinces. I gathered to myself male and female singers, and the delights of the sons of men—many concubines.
So I became great and surpassed all in Jerusalem who had preceded me; and my wisdom remained with me.
Anything my eyes desired, I did not deny myself. I refused my heart no pleasure. For my heart took delight in all my work, and this was the reward for all my labor.

Yet when I considered all the works that my hands had accomplished and what I had toiled to achieve, I found everything to be futile, a pursuit of the wind; there was nothing to be gained under the sun.
Then I turned to consider wisdom and madness and folly; for what more can the king's successor do than what has already been accomplished?
And I saw that wisdom exceeds folly, just as light exceeds darkness:
The wise man has eyes in his head, but the fool walks in darkness. Yet I also came to realize that one fate overcomes them both.
So I said to myself, "The fate of the fool will also befall me. What then have I gained by being wise?" And I said to myself that this too is futile.
For there is no lasting remembrance of the wise, just as with the fool, seeing that both will be forgotten in the days to come. Alas, the wise man will die just like the fool!
So I hated life, because the work that is done under the sun was grievous to me. For everything is futile and a pursuit of the wind.
I hated all for which I had toiled under the sun, because I must leave it to the man who comes after me.
And who knows whether that man will be wise or foolish? Yet he will take over all the labor at which I have worked skillfully under the sun. This too is futile.
So my heart began to despair over all the labor that I had done under the sun.
When there is a man who has labored with wisdom, knowledge, and skill, and he must give his portion to a man who has not worked for it, this too is futile and a great evil.
For what does a man get for all the toil and striving with which he labors under the sun?
Indeed, all his days are filled with grief, and his task is sorrowful; even at night, his mind does not rest. This too is futile.
Nothing is better for a man than to eat and drink and enjoy his work. I have also seen that this is from the hand of God.
For apart from Him, who can eat and who can find enjoyment?

To the man who is pleasing in His sight, He gives wisdom and knowledge and joy, but to the sinner He assigns the task of gathering and accumulating that which he will hand over to one who pleases God. This too is futile and a pursuit of the wind.

context.author: “The Teacher, the son of David, king in Jerusalem” (1:1); in Hebrew Qoheleth, “one who gathers” or “speaks to an assembly.” The book never names Solomon. Jewish and Christian tradition read it as Solomon; many scholars think a later writer took Solomon’s voice, because the Hebrew looks late and the speaker talks of kings before him in Jerusalem (1:16).
context.genre: Wisdom reflection: a searching first-person essay with poems and proverbs
context.audience: Anyone trying to find meaning in work, pleasure, wisdom and wealth, and finally “my son” (12:12)
context.setting: The Teacher runs an experiment on himself. He tries pleasure, laughter and wine (vv.1-3). He builds houses, plants vineyards, makes gardens and parks with fruit trees, and builds reservoirs to water them (vv.4-6). He gathers servants, herds, silver and gold, “the treasure of kings and provinces,” and singers (vv.7-8). “Anything my eyes desired, I did not deny myself” (v.10). Yet looking back over it all, he finds “nothing to be gained under the sun” (v.11). Wisdom is better than folly as light is better than darkness, but the wise man dies just like the fool (vv.13-16), and his work goes to someone who may be a fool (vv.18-21). He ends with the book’s first note of joy: “Nothing is better for a man than to eat and drink and enjoy his work… this is from the hand of God” (v.24).
context.custom: Kings in the ancient Near East boasted of their building projects, gardens and water works in their inscriptions. The word for “parks” in v.5 (pardes) is a Persian loanword, the source of the English word paradise. Royal gardens with pools stood south of Jerusalem’s City of David near the King’s Garden (Nehemiah 3:15; 2 Kings 25:4).
context.timelineImmediate: Chapter 3 sets out a time for everything, and says God has set eternity in human hearts.
context.timelineBible: Solomon’s wealth, buildings, horses and wives are described in 1 Kings 9-11, which also says his heart was turned away from the LORD in old age (1 Kings 11:4). Jesus tells of a rich man who built bigger barns and told himself, “Eat, drink, and be merry!” (Luke 12:19), but died that night.

translation.meaning: An orchard or walled park, a Persian word. Through Greek it became “paradise.”
“Chasing” or “shepherding” the wind. Trying to hold what cannot be held.
Good. Literally, to “see good” in his work. The good is God’s gift, not something seized.

gospelParallels.note: The rich fool: eat, drink, and be merry.
What will it profit a man if he gains the whole world?
God richly provides us with everything to enjoy.

otBackground.note: His wives turned his heart away.
When he dies he will carry nothing away.

overview.summary: The Teacher tries pleasure, great works and wealth, finds no lasting gain, sees that the wise die like fools, and yet calls eating, drinking and good work a gift from God.

history.t: Kings boasted of palaces, gardens and water works.

customs.t: A Persian word for park, later paradise.

archaeology.t: Pools at the south end of the City of David watered the king’s gardens.
Three large reservoirs south of Bethlehem bear Solomon’s name by tradition; they were built much later.

overview.discussion: The Teacher had everything his eyes desired and still found no gain (vv.10-11). What would I chase if I could have anything, and what does this chapter say about it?
overview.book: The book of Ecclesiastes · 12 chapters. The Teacher searches for lasting gain “under the sun,” finds everything a breath, and ends: fear God and keep His commandments.
overview.author: The Teacher (Qoheleth)

historicalImage.caption: The Tower of Babel, by Pieter Bruegel the Elder (1563, Vienna). A huge building project left unfinished, a picture of the Teacher’s great works that brought him no lasting gain (Ecclesiastes 2:4-11).
historicalImage.credit: Pieter Bruegel the Elder (1563), public domain / Wikimedia Commons

currentImage.caption: The Pool of Siloam at the south end of the City of David. The king’s gardens lay near here (Nehemiah 3:15), the kind of place the Teacher means: “I built reservoirs to water my groves” (Ecclesiastes 2:6). The steps seen today are from the time of Jesus.
